newsitem.title: USA: Fed watchers swayed more by data than by Greenspan.
newsitem.headline: Fed watchers swayed more by data than by Greenspan.

text.p: When forecasting U.S. monetary policy, Fed watchers proved to be more readily swayed by hard economic data than by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan's words of caution.

A Reuters poll taken after the strong February jobs data released on March , showed 17 out of 35 U.S. primary dealers expected the Fed to raise the 5.25-percent federal funds rate by 25 basis points when its Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) next meets on March 25.

This highlighted a substantial shift in sentiment from the February 27 Reuters poll taken right after the Humphey-Hawkins testimony where Greenspan warned about financial assets' overvaluation and wage-driven inflation risks.
In the February 27 poll, only five Fed watchers out of 35 forecast a March 25 rate hike. They were:
-- Joe Carson at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell
-- Sherry Cooper at Nesbitt Burns Securities
-- David Resler at Nomura Securities International
-- Stephen Roach at Morgan Stanley and Co.
-- Marc Wanshel at J.P. Morgan Securities
-- SBC Warburg's Ken Bercuson was also in that early tightening camp, though his forecast was not captured by the Reuters poll then.
These six Fed watchers based their forecast on Greenspan's hawkish Humphrey-Hawkins remarks made against the backdrop of an economy showing no sign of a slowdown.
Most Fed watchers who did not expect an early spring rate hike at the time argued inflation had not taken root yet.
But within 10 days, the buoyant February employment report led many economists to focus on Greenspan's comments about the need for preemptive policy. They now predict a March hike.

"A number of Fed watchers are looking for contemporaneous signs of inflation. They think the Fed won't act until inflation rises, which is not what Greenspan said," commented Ken Bercuson, head of research at SBC Warburg.
"It should be clear to anyone who is looking at the Fed what is happening. The weight of evidence is in one direction," Bercuson stressed.

"We're seeing no sign of a slowdown, imbalances are forming in financial and labor markets, demand is rising too strongly relative to supply. Everything that has been holding inflation down is coming to and end," Bercuson pointed out.
PNC Bank chief economist Stuart Hoffman agreed that Greenspan's remarks signaled "the die has been cast for the Fed to move in the spring," but were inconclusive regarding the timing.
"March 25, of course, is in the spring, so is May 20," added Hoffman in reference to the following FOMC meeting.
The PNC economist, who did not expect a move before May, explained that the employment report swayed many Fed watchers "because it's another sign of strength in the labor market."
The strength of the labor market -- 339,000 U.S. jobs created in February -- played a key role in Goldman, Sachs and Co chief economist William Dudley's March hike forecast.

Dudley, who had earlier dubbed the March meeting a very close call, predicted the Fed would begin tightening monetary policy at the March 25 FOMC meeting "because the economy continues to grow at an above-trend pace."
"Greenspan has not backed away from his earlier remarks that monetary policy needs to be preemptive and has clearly put Congress and the markets on notice," Dudley noted.

But Dean Witter Reynolds' senior vice president William Sullivan, who is forecasting a May rate hike, said the shift in sentiment about the Fed stemmed from "the environment that the Fed itself has created."

"They have sounded the theme for the last year or so that if the economy grows above its long-term 2.0- to 2.5-percent potential, they'll be willing to adjust policy. And when the economy grew above potential, the Fed still did not tighten," Sullivan said as to explain Wall Street's back-and-forth Fed policy forecasts over the past year.

"The perfect example is the chairman's attempt to talk about the equity market that involved convoluted logic and contradiction," Sullivan added. "They have created some confusion about what we should look at in the analytical community and the investing public."
